title: The end of the path (411–423)
hook: the one gone beyond both good and evil ties, bright as the moon, who has reached the end

segments.voice: Yesterday, paduma, and your line: in the water, not soaked by it. Today, the last verses of the book.
screen: `PADUMA — IN THE WATER, NOT SOAKED BY IT.`

segments.voice: The last page of a long book has its own feeling. You slow down. You read the final lines twice. Part of you wants it to go on, and part of you is proud you're here at all. Seventy-one days ago you opened the Dhammapada, and its first verse said: the mind comes first. Today come its last thirteen verses, four hundred eleven to four hundred twenty-three, and the book closes. It ends, fittingly, with a portrait of someone who has arrived.
screen: `THE LAST PAGE OF A LONG BOOK.` → `SEVENTY-ONE DAYS AGO: THE MIND FIRST.` → `A PORTRAIT OF ARRIVAL.`

segments.voice: The last verses finish the portrait of the brahmana, the one who has reached the end: no longings left, no doubts, the deathless touched. Then a surprising line: this one has gone beyond both good and evil, beyond the ties of both. It doesn't mean he stopped caring about goodness. The tradition reads it as going beyond the pull of both kinds of karma, good and bad, the fuel that keeps the wheel of rebirth turning. He is free of grief and stain, and the next verse compares him to the moon: bright, clear, serene, undisturbed. Then pictures you'll recognize. He has crossed the muddy, difficult road of rebirth and reached the far shore. His path can't be traced, the text says, not by gods or spirits or people, like the birds in the sky from chapter seven. He calls nothing his own, before, behind or in between, the words the acrobat Uggasena heard on his pole. And the last verse, four hundred twenty-three, describes the one who remembers his former lives, sees the heavens and the lower states, and has reached the end of births: a sage, complete. That's where the book stops. Not with a rule or a command, but with a picture of freedom. It began with a choice, the mind coming first, and pain following a bad thought like a wheel following an ox. It ends with the wheel standing still. Read it as a promise, a portrait or a direction to walk: you have now read the whole thing, twenty-six chapters, four hundred twenty-three verses.
screen: `BEYOND BOTH GOOD AND EVIL TIES.` · `BRIGHT, CLEAR, SERENE, LIKE THE MOON.` · `CROSSED OVER, PATH UNTRACEABLE.` · `THE END OF BIRTHS: A SAGE, COMPLETE.` · then, large: `THE END OF THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Let the whole book sit with you, and let a few pictures drift through as they come: the wheel following the ox, the bee and the flower, the deep still lake, the elephant bearing the arrow, the creeper, the emptied boat, the lotus leaf. Don't hold on to any of them; let each one arrive and roll off. Then let the pictures go, and just sit with the breath, at the end of the path.
Pāragū. One gone to the far shore: the book's last portrait is one who has crossed over, bright as the moon, with nothing left to cling to.
Your line: the wheel standing still. Whichever picture comes back on its own is yours. Day two hundred twenty-eight: the book is closed.

howItsDone: In Theravada tradition the brahmana chapter is read as a portrait of the arahant, one who has reached the end of the path; monks often chant the Dhammapada in full at special occasions, and many lay Buddhists read it through more than once.

original.note: Pali pāragū: one gone to the far shore; the brahmana chapter's word for someone who has crossed over.

trapdoor: what you thought: the end of the path means the end of the book.
what it means: the book's last portrait: one who has crossed over, free of clinging, a sage complete.

what a scholar hears: Theravada commentary reads the brahmana of chapter twenty-six as the arahant; verse 423 lists the three knowledges of the night of awakening: past lives, the passing of beings, the end of the taints.
recall: the root, where craving is cut with wisdom

notes: All verses paraphrased; Müller's wording of 412 ('above good and evil, above the bondage of both') and 423 could be quoted after checking SBE 10.
'Beyond good and evil' read as beyond both wholesome and unwholesome karma that leads to rebirth: standard Theravada reading; confirm.
Birds-in-the-sky image: verse 92 (chapter 7, day 176) and verse 420 here; the teach says 'chapter seven'.
Verse 421 echoes 348 (before, behind, between); the Uggasena link is the writer's connection, not the text's.
Seventy-one days: day 157 opened the book, day 158 read verse 1; day 228 is 71 days after 157. The hook counts from the opening day.
